Executive Case Study • Updated Sept 22, 2026

Solitaire for Low Vision

My mom plays solitaire on her iPhone. She has sight in one eye and floaters in the other, and commercial card games are cluttered with video ads and tiny corner indices. I led the end-to-end design and delivery of a custom, ad-free PWA built specifically for her eyes and hands.

My roleProduct Owner & Design Lead
EngineeringAI Ensemble (Claude, Codex, Antigravity)
PlatformiPhone 16e PWA (Offline-first)

The user and the problem

Seven columns, one small screen

Klondike needs seven columns side by side. My mother holds her phone upright one-handed, so all seven columns have to fit across a screen 390 points wide. That caps each card at roughly 51 points wide—about a third of an inch—and in cascading columns, the only part of most cards she can see is a thin strip at the top.

1 eye

Sight in one eye, floaters in the other. Contrast, scale, and clarity come before everything else.

390 pt

Screen width of an iPhone 16e, held in portrait the way she naturally plays.

7 cols

Classic 7-column Klondike layout, constraining each card to ~51 points wide.

1 look

The top peek strip of a covered card must convey rank, suit, and color unambiguously.

44 pt+

Minimum touch hitboxes with an 800ms double-tap window for deliberate, tremor-safe input.

How I ran it

Rules I set before anything was built

  • Options before decisions: Every visual element gets 5–6 distinct options rendered side-by-side. I pick one before code is built on top of it.
  • Never trust CSS math: Automated arithmetic lies on mobile viewports. Every layout change is rendered through headless WebKit/Chrome at true 390pt phone width and visually inspected.
  • Prevent destructive miss-taps: Solitaire players tap Undo repeatedly. Destructive actions (`New Game`) must never sit adjacent to high-frequency actions (`Undo`).
  • Zero unapproved changes: No speculative AI redesigns ship without explicit human review and sign-off.
  • Psychological safety: Deal #1 must be solver-verified and 100% winnable so her first experience is rewarding.
Design Leadership Overrides

Where I overrode the AI default

AI coding models consistently proposed textbook solutions that completely failed real-world accessibility and usability edge cases. Here are the key moments where human judgment overrode the machine:

AI Proposed

Adjacent `[New]` and `[Undo]` buttons in a shared top toolbar or 2+2 cluster.

My Override

Total physical isolation: New far left, Undo far right, ~38px empty safety buffer.

Why
"When mom explores moves, she spams Undo. If New is adjacent, she will misstap it. Even with a confirmation modal, interrupting flow causes anxiety. Physical separation makes accidental restarts impossible."
AI Proposed

A 28px vertical tableau cascade to pack more cards on screen.

My Override

Locked minimum 32px vertical step (The "Q-Tail" Rule).

Why
"At 28px, the card below covers the downward diagonal tail of the Queen. To someone with floaters, 'Q' reads identically to 'O'. 32px keeps the tail 100% visible."
AI Proposed

Double Happiness (`囍`) character on the card back for Chinese luck.

My Override

Pivoted to the Imperial Golden Dragon (金龍) 85% medallion.

Why
"Double Happiness is strictly a wedding motif in Hong Kong tradition. Testing with my Chinese wife caught that it felt absurd on playing cards. We explored 6 authentic motifs and selected the Imperial Dragon with a flaming ruby pearl."
AI Proposed

Clustered Sound, Timer, Score, Moves, and Menu buttons into one dense top bar.

My Override

Header stripped to stand-alone ovals; Score/Moves moved to bottom; Timer hidden by default; Sound in Menu.

Why
"Information overload. A low-vision player needs to focus on card stacks, not ticking clocks. Moving telemetry to the bottom and hiding the timer removes anxiety."
AI Proposed

Standard Unicode system emojis (`🎯`, `🃏`, `📦`, `💡`, `🔊`) in instructions and menus.

My Override

Bespoke inline vector SVGs matching the game's imperial gold and ruby aesthetic.

Why
"System emojis render as cartoonish multi-colored icons that look completely broken against our high-contrast felt table and Hong Kong theme. Bespoke SVGs preserve typographic dignity."
AI Proposed

Shrink the '10' slightly so its suit fits beside it on the card.

My Override

Every number stays the exact same size. Fit is solved via margins and suit bounds.

Why
"You cannot shrink the 10. In a low-vision game, having one rank print smaller than the rest degrades legibility. All numbers stay uniform, always."
Design rounds

Evolution from initial card to complete product

Every milestone was run through a side-by-side options bake-off rendered at the phone's true 390pt viewport width.

1

Card face typography

Five initial approaches to fitting a large number and suit into a 51pt card: side by side, stacked, color band, giant number, and classic enlarged corner.

What I caught: On device review, options B and E were unplayable: stacked cards covered the suit of the card behind them, and the "10" collided with its suit. I halted the round, had Claude fix the spacing, and established our mandatory true-width verification rule.

OutcomeSelected E's bold weight and opened Round 1b to refine layout.
1b-e

Uniform ranks, French Curve suits, and vector glyphs

When Claude quietly shrank the "10" to make it fit, I rejected it and set the permanent rule: all numbers stay one size. In Round 1c, we replaced bulky suits with elegant French Curve shapes (inward-curving diamonds, slender stems). Trimming empty viewBox padding gave us 40% more suit size in the same card width. Antigravity won the final card face bake-off by tracing the numbers into standalone SVGs so they render identically without font-loading flicker.

OutcomeCard face locked: traced SVGs, uniform rank sizing, French Curve suits.
2

Tableau spacing and the Queen's Tail

When testing full tableau deals, I noticed that tight vertical spacing caused the overlapping card to clip the lower stroke of the Queen. For someone with monocular floaters, an obscured Queen is indistinguishable from an 'O'. We rendered side-by-side vertical steps (26px, 28px, 30px, 32px, 34px). I locked the cascade at 32px, guaranteeing complete visibility of the Queen's tail across all 7 columns.

Rule LockedMinimum 32px tableau vertical step.
3

Waste pile fan overlap constraint

In Klondike, dealing from the stock into the waste pile requires fanning up to 3 cards horizontally. If the fan expands too wide, it encroaches on the tableau and foundation tap targets. We tested horizontal offsets from 18px to 32px. A 24px step proved optimal: clear visual separation of all three ranks with zero encroachment on adjacent columns.

OutcomeLocked 24px horizontal step for waste fan.
4

Cultural authenticity: The Imperial Dragon pivot

My mother was born and raised in Hong Kong. The initial AI build defaulted to the Double Happiness (囍) character on the card back. My Chinese wife immediately flagged that Double Happiness is exclusively a wedding motif and makes no sense on playing cards. I halted production and opened a studio of 6 authentic Hong Kong motifs (Imperial Dragon, Phoenix, Bat/Prosperity, Shou/Longevity, Wealth Coin, Endless Knot). I selected the Imperial Golden Dragon (金龍), then ran a second bake-off to enlarge the medallion to 85% card width with 36 sunburst notches and a flaming ruby pearl.

OutcomeImperial Golden Dragon locked across card backs, victory screens, and confirmation seals.
5

Accidental tap prevention & stand-alone oval geometry

Senior players frequently tap Undo multiple times in rapid succession. In standard apps, New Game sits right next to Undo. Miss-tapping New Game triggers a modal that interrupts the game and causes anxiety. I restructured the header layout into a 1fr auto 1fr grid: [＋ New] is locked to the far left, [↶ Undo] is locked to the far right, creating a ~38px physical buffer zone in between. Every button is an independent oval pill with a 2px gold border, 40px height, and clear textual labels (Menu, Help, New, Undo).

Ergonomic RulePhysical separation between high-frequency and destructive actions.
6

Cognitive load reduction & bottom telemetry HUD

Most solitaire games crowd the top bar with sound toggles, moving score counters, and ticking timers. For a player with low vision, visual motion in peripheral vision creates distraction. I removed sound from the top bar entirely and placed it inside Settings. I moved Score and Moves down to a floating brass status capsule docked at the bottom of the screen (`pointer-events: none` so cards remain clickable underneath), and hid the Timer by default to eliminate time pressure.

OutcomeQuiet header, floating bottom capsule, optional toggleable timer.
7

Hong Kong victory celebration & sky lanterns

When the game is won, the victory modal displays the identical Imperial Golden Dragon seal surrounded by 9 floating Chinese sky lanterns inscribed with auspicious blessings (龍, 福, 禄, 寿, 吉, 财, 旺, 春, 和), procedural gold particle bursts, and harmonious celebratory chords synthesized via the Web Audio API.

OutcomeCulturally resonant victory celebration matching deck aesthetic.
8

Psychological safety: The guaranteed winnable first deal

Standard Klondike Solitaire deals have an ~18-20% mathematical failure rate where no sequence of valid moves can unlock the tableau. Giving a low-vision senior an unwinnable deck on her very first game would be demoralizing. I engineered an algorithmic solver integration that guarantees Deal #1 is 100% solvable. Players can freely toggle between Guaranteed Winnable and standard Random deals in Settings.

OutcomeGuaranteed winnable first deal shipped, fostering immediate confidence.
Division of labor

Multi-AI orchestration: What the AI did, and what I did

AI Ensemble (Claude, Codex, Antigravity)

  • Codex: Scaffolded core engine logic, Deal 1/Deal 3 rules, and Service Worker caching.
  • Claude: Architected solver verification algorithms and state machine tests.
  • Antigravity: Rendered pixel-perfect vector SVGs, traced Didone card glyphs, and generated side-by-side design options studios.
  • Ran automated regression suites across viewports and simulated taps.

Shawn (Product Owner & Design Lead)

  • Defined the user constraints, physical touch parameters, and accessibility requirements.
  • Inspected every option on physical hardware at true 390pt scale.
  • Caught clipped Queen tails, obscured waste fans, and destructive button adjacencies.
  • Enforced cultural authenticity, overriding generic wedding symbols with the Imperial Dragon.
  • Made every single product, ergonomic, and aesthetic decision.

Strategic Takeaways

Lessons for Product & Design Leadership

This project illustrates three core principles for leading modern product teams in the age of generative AI:

1. Empathy

Accessibility is an innovation driver. Designing around severe real-world constraints (monocular vision, floaters, tremors) yielded a cleaner, faster, and more delightful product for all users.

2. Judgment

AI needs human taste and direction. AI can generate thousands of lines of syntactically correct code, but it cannot feel when an Undo button is dangerously close to New, or recognize cultural nuances. Taste remains human.

3. Physicality

Ergonomics happen at the physical edge. A few millimeters of button spacing or 4px of vertical cascade dictate whether software feels effortless or infuriating. Real-device verification is non-negotiable.
